topic: Memory Hierarchy and Caching Strategies: Full Range
explanation: The memory hierarchy is a tiered storage structure designed to mitigate the significant speed disparity between the CPU and main memory (DRAM). It organizes storage levels—registers, L1/L2/L3 caches, main memory, and secondary storage—by decreasing speed and increasing capacity. Caching strategies exploit the principle of locality of reference (temporal and spatial) by moving frequently accessed data blocks into faster, smaller cache levels. This mechanism ensures a high cache hit rate, drastically reducing the average memory access time (AMAT). Effective cache management, governed by policies for block placement (e.g., set-associative mapping) and replacement (e.g., LRU), is fundamental to maximizing system throughput and overall application performance.
